texts.150g-P6cP7f:
What impressed me most was how they think about authority. They call it mandar obedeciendo, leading by obeying. The representatives carry out what the assemblies decided, and they have to answer to the people who sent them.

The Zapatistas are also the closest thing to a whole example that I found, because their autonomy goes beyond how they vote. They've set up their own education and health care, and their own justice. They run their own collective production and political training. They've also worked out their own ways of teaching outsiders, all while coordinating beyond a single village.

texts.150g-P10aP11f:
Most institutions add layers and offices as they get older. The Zapatistas looked back at theirs and pushed authority down. Instead of putting out a leadership book and a certification program, they changed the system they were actually living in.

This is also where I have to rein in my enthusiasm. Zapatista autonomy grew out of Indigenous communities with long histories. They share language and family ties. They've fought land struggles together, and defended themselves together for decades. A new ecovillage can't copy the diagram everyone can see and get the trust underneath it right away.

texts.150g-P9fP10c:
After a long internal review, in 2023, the Zapatistas announced they were dissolving the Rebel Zapatista Autonomous Municipalities and the Good Government Juntas. Their new arrangement moved authority toward a Local Autonomous Government in each community. Those local governments can coordinate through regional collectives, but the coordinating levels are explicitly described as depending on the communities instead of sitting above them.

Most institutions grow more layers and offices the longer they're around. The Zapatistas went through theirs and pushed authority down to the communities. They didn't put out a leadership book or start some certification program. They just changed the system they were living in.
texts.150g-P11fP12c:
This is also where I have to rein in my enthusiasm. Zapatista autonomy grew out of Indigenous communities with long histories. They share language and family ties. They've fought land struggles together, and defended themselves together for decades. A new ecovillage can't copy the diagram everyone can see and get the trust underneath it right away.

One thing the Zapatistas have been clear about is that people shouldn't import or export Zapatismo as a ready-made model. It's okay to copy how they learn, though. They build things and ask questions, and when the practice isn't working the way it's supposed to, they change the structure.
texts.150g-P13c: I should also say the Zapatistas aren't proof of my whole economic path, the one that goes from unpriced internal necessities, to a common purse, to getting rid of outside money. Their communities do use collective work to support their schools and clinics, their autonomous government and their resistance. They also sell products and trade, and they receive outside support. What they've shown is that major necessities and public functions can come out of the market and be run collectively. Outside help can build a community's capability. But it can also create gatekeepers and uneven dependence, whenever the specialist, the donor or the organization stays indispensable.
texts.150g-P15a: One way an escuelita could fail is if it becomes a business, where people's lives turn into a performance of community for paying outsiders, and success gets measured by how many people come instead of how many daughter communities get started. A week of feeling transformed isn't what it's for. It's for teaching enough of the social and material system that some people can build it somewhere else.
texts.150g-P15b: An escuelita can fail by turning into a visitor business. The residents end up spending their lives performing community for outsiders who pay, and the number of guests becomes the measure of success instead of the number of daughter communities. Making people feel transformed for a week isn't the point. The point is teaching enough of the social and material system that some of them can go build it somewhere else.
texts.150g-P15e: A way an escuelita can fail is if it becomes a business in which people's lives are a performance of community life for paying outsiders, and its success is measured in how many people come, rather than how many daughter communities are started. It is not about providing a week of transformative experience, but about teaching people enough about how the social and material system works for some of them to be able to build one somewhere else.
texts.150g-P17c: Sociocracy, which comes out of a very different history, ended up with some of the same forms: circles, consent, distributed authority, and links between levels. That doesn't prove there's one universal formula. But it does give people building a community another serious system to study, so they're not inventing their governance in the middle of their first dispute.
